meaningMnemonic: First of all, there's a cross making up the middle, which automatically makes this a religion-based radical. That cross is the frame of someone's body and the things coming off of it are wings. This is an angel .

You see a little drop of something on your plate. Oh no… it's BLOOD !!! Yep, you're bleeding. Now you have to wash that plate again — just as soon as the bleeding stops. Don't worry, your platelets should stop the bleeding soon. Haha, get it? PLATE-lets? Like blood platelets? Japanese blood jokes.
This radical looks like the fire from the burner of a stove. That's because this is the boil radical. You need to boil a bunch of water over some flames.

Your leader ( ｲ ) has become a bent spoon ( 匕 ). Well, that's quite a change . Why would your leader transform like this? Maybe they're leading a movement of people transforming into spoons, like in protest or something. And why not? If you want to change the world, start by changing yourself. Into a spoon.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means city . In case you don't remember the kanji's meaning mnemonic, here's a refresher: You see a manhole lid and a towel , both with the name of a city on them. Decorative manhole lids and souvenir towels — two things cities love to slap their names on, especially in Japan.

There's a lid on a lion. And you're stuck under the lid with the lion, which means you will surely meet your death . Or if you don't want to die, think of the poor lion. If you leave a lion under a lid for too long, death will come for it too. Either way, somebody's gonna die today.
Behind that tree the sun is rising in the east . The sun always rises in the east, so if you head that way, past the tree, you'll be going east too.
You put on your hat and go outside to kick something white. It's a big white goose and you killed it with your kick. That's because you're going to cook and eat it. Yum!

Someone has a toe in their mouth. She's a fortune teller telling your fortune . But for her to do it, she has to take one of your toes and taste it. This better be a good fortune for you to let her put your foot in her mouth.

This is a tree with a drooping slide shape on top. What causes the top of plants to sag? The grain s. Imagine seeing how the heads of wheat or rice droop when they're ready for harvest. It will look like this radical. Look at all that ripe grain! This might remind you of 米 , which has three stalks sprouting upward. You can tell the difference because the top of this one is slanted from the weight of the ripe grain.

Under this roof is a pig with her little ones. Your pig, because it's your house ! You keep your piggies inside where it's nice and warm. They're all members of your family, so they deserve to live in your house too.
This is like one of those jet s that have little nose-wings. Imagine you're looking at the jet from the top down: this is what it would look like. It's also why this is the jet radical.
This is a knife . See the sharp edge on the left and the tapered tip on top? And there's a little handle at the bottom for the... well, the handle. Be careful you don't cut yourself on this knife!
There's a ladle scooping up two drops of liquid. See the handle and the scoop part of the ladle? Imagine ladling some water into your mouth. Mmm.

This L-shaped radical is the lion radical, because "L" is for "Lion." It also looks like a lion's mouth being opened really, really wide. Imagine a lion opening its mouth to yawn. It looks like this radical!
When a stick figure has hair that drags on the ground and gets kicked all the time, you know that hair's gotta be long . Why is it so looooong?!

This radical is just like the katakana character "ma" ( マ ). So let's keep things simple and make the radical mama . It even looks like a mama leaning over and gently tapping her baby to help them fall asleep.
This is the radical for neck . Look, you can see all the vertebrae stacked up, and the little ligaments that connect it to the base of the skull! That's why this is the radical for neck.
This is a very fluffy sheep . See the two horns poking up and all its wool poking out to the side? It's so fluffy that you can hardly see its tiny little legs. What a cute sheep!

This is the tongue radical. See that sturdy slide holding a thousand people above a mouth? An open mouth can't support that much weight, but a strong tongue can — it's the muscle of the mouth, after all. Alternatively, you can think of this as something sticking out of a mouth with thousands of tiny taste buds on it. It's your tongue!

This radical looks like a yakuza . See him facing left, with that threatening jawline and big pompadour hairstyle? Maybe imagine a couple scars on his face too. You know, real yakuza-like. You could also remember this because it's the evening radical under the ground radical, and people who do stuff underground in the evening (or night) are definitely yakuza.

The hat crowns the king , because all kings must have one. Hints Think of as many kings as you can think of. Guess what? Literally all of them wear hats! Think of strange hats, funny hats, normal hats, and crowns. Just make sure you're amazed by the fact they're all wearing them.
readingMnemonic: But, as you're going through all the kings, it turns out not all of them have hats after all. The last one you come to is hatless. He's the king of Zen ( ぜん ). He has simple clothes and a shaved head, unlike all the other fancy kings standing around nearby. Hints To add to this story and make it more memorable, you can imagine the other kings getting upset, saying things like "All kings must wear hats! You are no king!" The king of Zen Buddhism just ignores them and begins to meditate.

meaningMnemonic: If you loiter around to poop in winter you never know what could be happening behind you. After you're done you could turn back to see something really crazy that you missed because you took so long to poop in the cold. Hints Imagine trying to loiter while you poop in the winter. You're just trying to take your time as you squat over the snow, but soon you hear things behind you.
readingMnemonic: You finally look behind you and see Go dzilla ( ご ) and a giant こう いち having a violent battle back there! Hints Godzilla and こういち were going at it behind you the entire time you were just lazily taking a poop in the snow?! Ahh, that's so embarrassing! And also dangerous, they could have crushed you! You should look behind you more.

meaningMnemonic: The blood radical and blood are the same in looks as well as in meaning. Hints There'll be some bad blood between us if you're not studying your radicals, especially when they're the same like this kanji!
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading けつ , we use the word "ketsup." The perfect mix of ketchup and catsup! The radical is technically blood , but you know that radical is just a drop (of blood) on a plate. So, you ask yourself... Is that really blood on the plate? Could it be? You decide to take a gamble and lick it off. When you taste it, it's definitely not blood. No, it's ketsup ( けつ ). Hints Feel the relief that you didn't just lick up someone's blood. Taste the ketsup taste, too. It's pretty good. Not quite ketchup, but not quite catsup. Yum!

meaningMnemonic: As you dig under the ground you discover a head resting near a mountain , which are both strange things to find beneath the earth. Hints You'll want to focus on the part where you find both, not so much the things themselves. Think about how you can't believe you did so well finding both things at once. Usually you only find one or the other when you're searching.
readingMnemonic: But, you dig too deep and water flows into where you are. Your only hope is a row ( りょう ) boat floating off in the distance. Hints Also think... "What's that row boat doing here?" But, it's your only hope, so you have to focus on it really hard.

meaningMnemonic: The change radical and change kanji are exactly the same. Except this kanji can also mean transform . But that's just another kind of change, isn't it? Hints Radicals be like "this isn't even my final form," then proceed to change into an identical kanji with readings and additional meanings you have to learn.
readingMnemonic: Imagine your country's leader taking this spoon and whispering some magic words to it to change it into a car ( か ). Hints Feel amazed at seeing a spoon transform into a car. Like, really imagine it, otherwise it'll be hard to remember the kanji reading later. If you feel amazed now, you'll always know that spoons changing into cars means the reading is か .

meaningMnemonic: The mouth of the king extends all the way around him (like in this kanji). Where his mouth reaches, that is his country , give or take a few drop s. Hints Imagine his talking taking physical form. As he talks, waves extend out from him, and stop right at the border of his country before getting to the next one.
readingMnemonic: Turns out the king of this country loves drinking Coke ( こく ). Every morning that big mouth of his swallows a whole 2-liter bottle of Coke for breakfast. Hints Would you drink that much soda for breakfast? Now this king says he wants to pass a law requiring everyone in the country to drink nothing but Coke! That's crazy!

meaningMnemonic: The radical death and the kanji death are the same. Hints This thing is deceased. It ain't alive anymore.
readingMnemonic: Your death will be because of a bow ling ( ぼう ) accident. Oh, you didn't know? You're going to be hit by a giant bowling ball and crushed flat. Hints You didn't want to know what would cause your death, you say? Well that's a shame. I guess you could try to avoid bowling from now on, but that won't do any good. Mark my words, your death will be bowling-related.

meaningMnemonic: If the yakuza hands you a spoon , death is coming for you. It's the death spoon, a sign that the yakuza is coming to cause your death. Hints This spoon isn't for pudding, it's for death!
readingMnemonic: Death comes in the form of a shee p ( し ). The death sheep works for the yakuza, and kills anyone who has their spoon. Hints Picture the death sheep. He looks like a black shadow, and he has a scar on his face. He's holding a bunch of spoons, from all the other people the yakuza marked for death!

meaningMnemonic: A dirt alligator lives in the earth , not the water. They can swim through the earth itself! Which is pretty scary. You can think of this word as ground too, because that's kind of what earth is made of. Hints Imagine seeing the earth moving as a dirt alligator rises out from the ground. You should run.
readingMnemonic: The only way to keep this dirt alligator from dragging you under the earth and eating you is to feed it chee se ( ち ). That way it won't lead you to a horrific death under the earth by dragging you under and spinning you around until you eat dirt (literally). Hints If you ever see someone throwing cheese on the ground, now you know why. They aren't crazy, they're saving us humans from what's lurking under the earth.

meaningMnemonic: This is the same as the radical for east , so it means east too. Hints Remember the radical mnemonic? The sun rises behind that tree in the east!
readingMnemonic: You see a man walk straight toward the sun rising in the east . It's so bright he can't see anything, so he trips and he gash es ( ひがし ) his knee on a rock. Yikes… But he gets back up, determined to head east, and, oh no, he gashes his other knee! OK, he should probably give up on going east. Hints Imagine the secondhand pain you'd feel watching him as he gashes his knee. Ow… Surely nothing in the east can be worth that much suffering?

meaningMnemonic: The radical for eat and the kanji for eat are the same! Lucky you. Hints If you know the radical, you basically know the meaning(s) of this kanji. There is a second meaning added to it, though, and that is meal . Just think about the things you eat? What are they? In the simplest form, they are just meals. So, if you know "eat" you should be able to remember "meal" as well.
readingMnemonic: Thank goodness, you finally get to eat your meal . You're so hungry. Someone has been starving you and now they've finally given you food. Unfortunately, though, every time you take a bite, you get a shock ( しょく ) from somewhere. Hints So, do you keep eating and keep getting shocked? Or do you not eat and continue to starve? What is worse? Obviously you're in one of the Saw movies, or something, too, so feel the fear. What will you choose? Life with shocks or death from hunger?

meaningMnemonic: There are some horns on the ground and a moon knife in front of you. When you try to move, they always rotate around with you, staying right in front. You can't escape these objects, for some reason. This kanji means before too. Something that's in front of you is before you, after all. Hints Perhaps it's some kind of magic, but you don't care. Why are these strange objects always in front of me? Why won't they stay put? This will get pretty freaky after a while. Try to run. Try to hide. Spin around. Do whatever you need to do. No matter what, these objects are always in front.
readingMnemonic: You're going crazy with these things in front of you all the time. You finally seek the help of a Zen ( ぜん ) master, who tells you that meditation will save you from this curse. You try it out, and sure enough, the objects are gone! It worked! Hints Go ahead and do some Zen Buddhist meditation. Maybe it'll help you to remember this kanji's reading better (and calm your mind so you're ready for the next kanji!).

meaningMnemonic: A narwhal and a moon are all you have . Imagine one of each under your arms. Hints You don't have anything else. This is it. All you have.
readingMnemonic: Everything you have (except the narwhal and the moon) were taken from you by a roving gang of you ths ( ゆう ). Hints They came and took your things. Now they have all your stuff, and you only have the moon and a narwhal. You don't have much anymore, but at least you have these things still.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical, so it means house . Or home , since most houses are someone's home too. Hints I guess not all houses are homes, and not all homes are houses. But there's a pretty big overlap, right? And in most situations, this kanji's got you covered.
readingMnemonic: What do you do in your house ? You ea t e ggs ( いえ ), that's what. You eat eggs three times a day, every day. You really love eating eggs in your home ! Hints Imagine all the eggs you've got in your house. Whole fridgefuls! It's not a normal house, but that's okay. If you couldn't eat eggs, it wouldn't feel like home.

meaningMnemonic: Your private grain s are meant to stay private ! You shouldn't be sharing them with the whole town, they're just for you. This kanji also means I . Why? Because what's more private than you? I mean, I! Basically, some things are only the business of you (I) and those things should be private. Hints Look at your private grains. Who are those for? Why, they're for I!
readingMnemonic: You're getting into the zone, thinking about yourself ( I ) and how much you love having things that are private and just yours, when you realize there is a shee p ( し ) in this grain bag. And it's eating all of your (I's) private grains. No! Hints The moral of the story is: don't let a sheep sneak into your private stash of things just for you (I). I'm sure this is a metaphor for something important...

meaningMnemonic: You take an arrow to the mouth because you know too much. You know some very sensitive information, and someone's sent a bow-slinging enforcer to pin your big blabbermouth shut with arrows. Hints Think of all the important things you know that you were hoping to blab about: JFK's real killer, the truth about Area 51, Koichi's shocking connections to the Illuminati. You better hurry and get this arrow out of your mouth so you can tell the world what you know.
readingMnemonic: One of the things you know too much about is the shee p ( し ) plan for world domination. Yes, you know that sheep are in fact plotting to overthrow humanity and take over the world. Hints Take a closer look at that bow-slinging thug who fired the arrow into your mouth. Their shadowy silhouette looks awfully… woolly, doesn't it? It's undeniable: the sheep are trying to shut you up.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami of tongue s is coming at you. As it washes over you, you feel each individual tongue moving around on your body, licking you. They make you feel so... lively ! Hints Your entire body wakes up, you feel so lively! The tongues are making you more aware of yourself and your surroundings than you've ever been. You want to dance, you want to sing, you want to live your life.
readingMnemonic: This lively feeling isn't just happening to you, the tongue tsunami is licking it into all of the cats ( かつ ) in your neighborhood too! Hints You and the cats are running around playing together, because you can't seem to get the lively feelings to stop. You have to get the energy out, but the cats have sharp claws and they're scratching you.

meaningMnemonic: The long radical and the long kanji are the same! This kanji also means leader , because the longer a person is, the better a leader they'll be. Or maybe it was... the longer they've been somewhere? Whatever, longness = leaderness, you know? Hints As long as you know the radical long, you know the kanji long as well.
readingMnemonic: You see a very long person. It's Mrs. Chou ( ちょう ), who has made herself long, like her street. "I made myself long so I can watch more of the street, my domain. I'm the leader of these streets. Watch yourself not-long person," says Mrs. Chou. Hints Long isn't an idea that's easy to imagine in any specific sense, but you can try some other things too, as long as it gets associated with Mrs. Chou . For the most part, when you see a kanji with the radical 長 the reading will be ちょう .

meaningMnemonic: There are mouth s, twenty of them, singing beautiful music together. The music seems to bend toward you through the air. Hints Listen to the mouths. All twenty of them. They sound great. Have them sing your favorite music. Imagine the music coming at you, bending all around in strange shapes through the air.
readingMnemonic: The twenty mouths make so much music that they literally cloak you ( きょく ) with it. They cloak you with the music. Hints Imagine how you feel as they cloak you with music. Feel the music all around you, enveloping you. Become the music itself.

meaningMnemonic: The radical neck and the kanji neck are exactly the same!
readingMnemonic: The only thing you do with your neck is use it to swallow lots of coo l bea ns ( くび ). Mm mm. Feel those cool, cool beans sliding down your neck. You don't really taste them, but you know they're there. Hints Look at yourself in a mirror as the cool beans make their way down your neck. You can see them, like little ants marching all the way down to your tummy.

meaningMnemonic: The only woman in this city is your older sister . She's the only woman surrounded by a bunch of men, but she's following her dreams in the big city. Hints You want to go to the city someday, but you're not old enough yet, like your older sister is.
readingMnemonic: Your older sister may have moved to the city, but she kept her pet shee p ( し ) with her. Now the only woman in the city is your older sister, and the only sheep is her pet. Hints Picture your older sister and her sheep walking through the city. Everyone turns to stare at them, because they're the only ones of their kind.

meaningMnemonic: Your fortune boil s down to a single point in time. One point in time determines how the rest of your future will go. Hints Imagine actually going somewhere to get your fortune told and watching a big boiling pot of goo. As it boils, it melts down to a single point at the very bottom. Where this point is determines your future.
readingMnemonic: As you stare at the point , you watch in awe as it moves to the ten ( てん ) spot in a long series of numbers. Hints Is the ten spot good? Are you going to live a long life or does this point mean you're only going to live ten more years?! Ahh!

meaningMnemonic: With a roof over her head, a woman can relax . She doesn't have to worry about rain or snow or finding a place to sleep. The roof also happened to be super cheap , so she can even relax about her finances. Hints Picture the super relaxed woman lounging under her cheap but sturdy roof. Ah, she doesn't have a care in the world!
readingMnemonic: As she relax es, she pulls out the cheap est, most relaxing food in the world: an chovies ( あん ). Hints Think about it: anchovies cost next to nothing, they come in cans, you don't have to cook them or cut them up. You just munch them down. There's nothing more cheap and relaxing than eating anchovies under your own roof.

meaningMnemonic: You put a roof over the ground to make your own private patch of dirt . This is your room ! That's really all a room is, you know? A covered, private place where you can have some time to yourself. Hints Imagine the room you live in now. Take away all the stuff and you're left with a roof above the ground. Your own little private place atop the dirt.
readingMnemonic: The only problem with your room is that you can't always be alone. Because of your dad's shih tzu ( しつ ). The shih tzu likes to come into your room and pee everywhere. Ruining your privacy completely. Hints Imagine watching the little shih tzu come into your room and lift its leg to all your things. This isn't fair. The shih tzu has its own room to pee in. Why does it have to ruin yours?

meaningMnemonic: You scoop some grain s into a ladle to do science . You're doing experiments on these grains in your science course . Hints Imagine carefully ladling grains into different piles so you can do science experiments on them. This course is going to make you an expert. You'll be the best in this department!
readingMnemonic: Using your science skills, the right temperatures and measurements, you manage to get these grains to grow into a ca r ( か ). This is the science department 's special car now! Hints From your science meddling, these grains grow huge, red, and sprout sports cars when they're ripe. This is the true power of science!

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami is coming, so you point your gun out the window at it. "You better turn back, sea , or I'll shoot!" Hints You'll have to think of the "sea" as its own entity, controlling the tsunami, otherwise you might confuse and combine the two. So when you point your gun out the window, aim it at the "sea," not the "tsunami." It's like aiming for the head of a zombie and not the arms or legs.
readingMnemonic: The sea decides it doesn't want to die today, so it turns its tsunami around and goes the other way. You hop in your kay ak ( かい ) and chase after it with your gun, to make sure it actually returns to the sea and doesn't just drown someone else. Hints Imagine paddling in your kayak, your gun still in one hand, as you chase the sea back to its home.

meaningMnemonic: The sheep radical and the sheep kanji are the same in looks as well in meaning. Hints You are no sheep—you study your radicals, unlike most Japanese learners. You'll learn sooo much faster!
readingMnemonic: To remember よう , we use the word "Yogurt." The sheep are after you. There are too many of them, and they're chasing you down, stalking you... because you stole their sheep's milk yo gurt ( よう ). Now you're running and crying and trying to eat the yogurt before the sheep catch up and stomp you down with their hooves. Hints Imagine the taste of this yogurt. You're scared and tired from running, but it tastes great!

meaningMnemonic: A long time ago, someone put up a canopy over their fortune telling booth and created the first shop . This store was fortune-based, but since then lots of different stores have popped up! Hints Picture the very first store in history. A fortune teller decided enough was enough, they should be in some kind of structure where it's safe, official looking, and more permanent.
readingMnemonic: This shop quickly turned into ten ( てん ) shops! It was a good idea, after all, so all of the other people selling goods and services decided to copy it and create their own shops. The next day there were ten more. Hints Picture ten shops, all made up of someone selling something under a canopy. The first one is the fortune teller, but the nine others are whatever you want them to be!

meaningMnemonic: The sun that gives life is our very own star (which we happen to call the sun). Of course, all the other stars are probably giving life to other planets as well. Hints Imagine all sorts of stars all around the universe giving life to planets as suns. These are all the stars you see in the sky and there are billions of them. I hope you don't feel overwhelmed by how minuscule we really are when you look up at all of them.
readingMnemonic: "All these life-giving star s need a protector," you say, pulling out your sa ber ( せい ). It's a big responsibility, but with your trusty saber in hand, you're sure you can defend our star system. Hints Now you're soaring amongst the stars, swinging your saber at all manner of cosmic foes, and... wait. No, that was a dream. You roll over and pat your saber. The two of you are ready just in case the stars need your help.

meaningMnemonic: Think about Japan. Japan is a country made up of islands. They're basically three drop drop drop s in the large river that is the Pacific Ocean. These are Japan's state s or province s. Hints Also, another way to think of this is that the river radical is actually just three rivers, separating drops, which are capitals of various states. Rivers are usually great ways to divide up a country, and states are one way to do it!
readingMnemonic: Each state has its own shoe ( しゅう ) to represent it. The bottom of each shoe is the shape of the state, so when you step it leaves a state-shaped imprint in the ground. Hints The state shoes also have things like the state birds, state flowers, and state fish printed on each of them. They're quite collectable, you should buy a pair for your favorite state!

meaningMnemonic: There's an ear just sitting on a stool . Nobody's watching, so, you take it. Hints Feel the rush of stealing something (even though it's a weird something, admittedly). Start walking away quickly. You don't want to get caught!
readingMnemonic: You're the kind of person who likes to take things. "What things?" you ask. Little toe s ( と ). Because that isn't creepy. Hints When someone asks you "Do you like to take little toes?" your answer is always "Toetally."

meaningMnemonic: If you can steal the flowers that adorn a hat worn by an angel , you can use them to make delicious tea . Naturally, angels decorate their hats with only the most aromatic and delicious flowers fit for brewing. Hints Imagine wrestling with an angel for its flowery hat, then running home with it. Success! Oh yes, this tea is going to taste… heavenly . *rimshot*
readingMnemonic: After brewing the tea , you look at the hat again and find a nametag inside that says Cha d ( ちゃ ). You decide that from now on this tea variety will be known as Chad tea, in honor of Chad. Hints For some reason knowing the angel's name makes you feel extra guilty. Chad the angel, flowerless and hatless... Oh well. At least its name lives on in this heavenly tea.

meaningMnemonic: In a rice paddy you find a heart and it makes you think . You think a lot of thought s like, "Whose heart is this? Why is it in a rice paddy? Why am I thinking out loud?" Hints Think, think, think. Think about this rice paddy heart.
readingMnemonic: As you are think ing these thought s, you spot someone on the edge of the rice field. He really reminds you of someone. But who? That's it! He reminds you of that bartender on The Simpsons. What's his name? You think some more. What is it? Oh! Moe ( おも ) is his name! Hints If you don't know Moe from the Simpsons use a different Moe, perhaps the one from the Three Stooges? You should be able to come up with one. Think really hard about the Moe you know best and imagine them standing watching you from the edge of the rice field.

meaningMnemonic: You stop at a small slide . What were you doing before you stopped here? You were walk ing. Hints Question is, what made you stop? Imagine yourself walking at a nice casual pace... then imagine something that would make you stop that's incredibly interesting and strange. Maybe an alien is going down the slide? He would say "keep walking, friend."
readingMnemonic: So, you're walk ing around, minding your own business, when suddenly something flips up and whacks you in the face. You stepped on the head of a hoe ( ほ ) and it caused it to swing up from the ground and hit you. Hints Of course, imagine the pain of your face. Did your nose break? After bringing yourself together, look down at what hit you. It's a hoe! How did you manage to step on just the right spot to flip it up on you like that? Examine the hoe. Pay close attention to it. Whose hoe is this? etc.

meaningMnemonic: A drop hits your mustache . Where did it come from? "Ah, it came from yonder ," you say, facing that way. Hints Yonder is a bit of a weird word, but it fits the meaning of this kanji quite well. You'll have to trust me that it's more useful in Japanese than it is in English. When you imagine this mnemonic, make sure the drop comes from the side and hits you in the mustache with quite a bit of force. That means it came from a far distance, thus making you look over "yonder."
readingMnemonic: Who shot this drop at you from yonder ? You look over yonder, and see a figure. It is こう いち . Hints "Who is that over yonder!" you yell. "It is I, こういち ," he yells back. "I shot at you over yonder because you weren't doing your kanji reviews often enough and you're taking up space on our database." "But I'm paying you!" "Oh, that's true. Well, I'm going to walk over yonder and leave you alone, then."

meaningMnemonic: Who's that woman pretending to be a jet ? That's my younger sister . *Sigh* Hints Imagine a little girl (your younger sister) running around with her arms out, pretending to be a jet, too. Prwoooooo!
readingMnemonic: Your younger sister is giving some mi ce ( まい ) a ride on her back like a jet. Hints Ew, gross. Your younger sister is such a weirdo! Why does she have mice on her back while pretending to be a jet?

meaningMnemonic: This shares one of the meanings you learned for the kanji: after . You can differentiate this one from 後ろ (which you may or may not have seen yet) thanks to the で on the end. Some people believe that after something's dead ( で ), it goes to an afterlife.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: After . Everything happens after. It's a cause and effect chain. One thing happens, and then another thing happens after. This is life. This is the universe. Everything is after. It's an auto matic ( あと ) cycle that just keeps going and going and going.

sentences.japanese: 後でホテルに来て下さい。
sentences.english: Please come to the hotel later.

sentences.japanese: ミーティングについては後でメールしますよ。
sentences.english: I will email about the meeting later.

meaningMnemonic: This has a little hiragana attached to it but nothing that suggests it's a verb or an adjective. That means you can assume this word has the same meaning as its parent kanji.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You wanted to remember everything about your trip, so you bought every souve nir ( すべ ) available in the entire shop to ensure you had all the mementos possible.

sentences.japanese: 玉ねぎは全て切りますか？
sentences.english: Should I cut this entire onion?

sentences.japanese: 全ての人は、人から生まれました。
sentences.english: Every person was born from a person.

meaningMnemonic: You know 日本 means "Japan." So, now you have the kanji for all added to it, making this word All Japan (as in "All Japan Railways" or something like that).
readingMnemonic: You know the reading of 日本 . Now just add the on'yomi reading of 全 and you should be able to read this word.

sentences.japanese: 全日本の人口は主にアジア人です。
sentences.english: The population of all of Japan is mainly Asian.

sentences.english: The All Japanese women's volleyball team is good.

sentences.japanese: 全日本の山の中でも、ふじ山は人気です。
sentences.english: Mt. Fuji is popular among all the mountains in Japan.

meaningMnemonic: You have something that's before (or in front of) noon . What is before noon? That is AM .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 平日の午前はランニングをします。
sentences.english: I run in the morning on weekdays.

sentences.japanese: 午前中のミーティング、どうだった？
午前１０：００、ホテルの入り口にはカメラマンがたくさんいました。
sentences.english: At 10:00 am, there were many photographers at the hotel entrance.

meaningMnemonic: What is the neck of your leg ? Think about it. It's your ankle .
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings from both kanji, probably because it includes body parts. You know the kun'yomi reading of 足 from previous vocab and you know the kun'yomi reading of 首 from learning that kanji. So, you should be able to read this kanji so long as you remember that it's all kun'yomi.

sentences.japanese: 足首のストレッチをしましょう。
ハイヒールをはいて、足首がいたくなった。
sentences.english: I wore high heels and my ankles became sore.

sentences.japanese: 大きい山でハイキングするときは、足首をケガしないようにね。
sentences.english: When you hike on a large mountain, don't injure your ankle.

meaningMnemonic: If there's a ca r ban ( カバン ), you'll need a nice bag to carry all your stuff in. You can't just throw it all in the car, so get yourself a nice bag instead. カバン is used for bags that you can close and that have a fairly rigid structure, like satchels or briefcases, but not more flimsy bags that don't close, like plastic or paper shopping bags. This word can also be written in hiragana and kanji. All versions are pretty common, but you'll probably see it in katakana the most.

sentences.english: to snatch a bag from someone
to put something in a bag
to put something away in a bag
to take something out of a bag
to take out of a bag
something comes out of a bag
Oh, I don't have my bag!

sentences.japanese: おかしいなぁ。カバンに入れたはずなのに。
sentences.english: That's funny. I thought I put them in my bag.

sentences.japanese: いっぱい入るよう、大きめのカバンにしたよ。
sentences.english: I opted for a larger bag that can hold a lot of stuff.

meaningMnemonic: The hiragana attached to this word doesn't suggest it's a verb or an adjective, so we can assume it's a noun. While 後で (you may or may not have seen this word yet) means "after," this one means all the other meanings you learned with the kanji: behind , back , and rear . Think of the ろ as a hint. It's like saying you're on the "road" ( ろ ) and you're driving so fast you're leaving everything "behind."
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Continue to think you're driving on this road. You hit something, then look behind you, seeing you hit a cow. Know the word for cow in Japanese? It's うし , which is also the reading for this word.

sentences.english: to look behind, to look back
the two people in the back

sentences.japanese: 後ろに見える大きな山が、ふじ山です。
sentences.english: The big mountain you can see behind is Mt. Fuji.

sentences.japanese: 車の後ろのシートにティッシュがあります。
sentences.english: There is a tissue on the back seat of the car.

sentences.japanese: 人々の後ろに一人女の人が立っています。
sentences.english: A woman is standing behind people.

meaningMnemonic: When the thing that is exit ing is blood , you are probably bleeding .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Note that the しゅつ from 出 gets shortened to しゅっ . That's a small つ there, not a big one.

sentences.japanese: まだ両手に出血があります。
sentences.english: There is still bleeding on both hands.

sentences.japanese: 出血がひどくて、大した力も出せなかった。
sentences.english: The bleeding was so bad that I couldn't use much power.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You cut yourself and there's blood everywhere. You need to stop the bleeding with something, but the only thing nearby is a block of chee se. You grab the cheese and stuff it into your gash, but the blood comes out the holes (it is Swiss cheese, blargh!). Imagine this in great detail to be able to remember it well.

sentences.english: to shed blood, to spill blood
to cough up blood, to spit out blood
to bleed, to have blood flowing
to be muddied with blood, to be bloodstained

sentences.japanese: シャツに血がついていますよ。
sentences.english: There is blood on your shirt.

sentences.japanese: うわ、足首から血が出てる！
sentences.english: Yikes, blood is coming out of my ankle!

sentences.japanese: 父は、私と血がつながってません。
sentences.english: My father is not related to me by blood.

meaningMnemonic: Here you have both direction s / way s. Every time you have to choose between something it's like having to choose between two ways. That's why this word is simply both . Close to the kanji is the meaning both sides , as well. Learn either for 両方 , they're pretty similar.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 父も母も、両方ともフランス人です。
sentences.english: Both my father and mother are French.

sentences.japanese: 両方の手を力いっぱい上げて下さい。
sentences.english: Please raise both your hands with as much power as possible.

sentences.japanese: 両方とも私のかき氷です。

meaningMnemonic: Kanji doesn't go together much better than this. Both plus day equals both days . This is a bit of a formal word though, you'll hear important people say it more than your friends.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 日 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: On both days of your vacation, you get two boats to row ! Gee, two ( りょうじつ ) boats at once? Try not to fall in!

sentences.japanese: 両日のスケジュールをメールして下さい。
sentences.english: Please email the schedule for both days.

sentences.japanese: 両日とも雨になるそうですよ。
sentences.english: It looks like it'll rain on both days.

sentences.japanese: ごめんなさい。両日とも、ミーティングが入っています。
sentences.english: Sorry. There are meetings on both days.

meaningMnemonic: Don't use one hand when you can use both hands . This is simply both plus hand put together. It can also mean both arms .
readingMnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with both kanji. No problemo for a kanji master such as yourself.

sentences.japanese: 両手を上げて、バンザイをしました。
sentences.english: They raised both hands and shouted banzai.

sentences.japanese: 女の子は両手を広げてストレッチをした。
sentences.english: The girl spread her arms and stretched.

sentences.japanese: スクリーンを見ないで両手でタイピングできる人がタイプなんです。
sentences.english: My type is the person who can type with both hands without looking at the screen.

meaningMnemonic: What is the color of tea ? You'd think it would be green, assuming it's Japanese... but this word came from China. What color is Chinese tea? It tends to be more brown . Think Oolong tea, for example.
readingMnemonic: The readings for both kanji are the readings you learned with the kanji, meaning you should be able to read this already.

sentences.japanese: 私のカバンは茶色です。
茶色の毛の牛はレストラン用です。
sentences.english: Brown haired cows are for restaurants.

sentences.japanese: 明るい茶色にカラーリングしたいんですけど。
sentences.english: I'd like to color my hair bright brown.

meaningMnemonic: You’ve already learned 仕方 , which you know means "method" or "way of doing." When you don’t (that’s the がない part) have a way of doing or achieving something, you could say it can’t be helped , it’s no use , or there’s no other way . Makes sense, right? This is a popular phrase in Japanese, so we're sure you'll encounter it a lot!
readingMnemonic: You already know how to read this from having learned 仕方 , so you should be good to go!

sentences.japanese: そこにずっと立っていても仕方がないよ。
sentences.english: It's no use even if you kept standing over there.

sentences.japanese: フライトがなくて日本に来られないのは仕方がない。
sentences.english: There's nothing you can do about coming to Japan when there's no flight available.

sentences.japanese: 雨の日が少なかったんだから、今年の水不足は仕方がないよ。
sentences.english: There were not many rainy days, this year's water shortage couldn't be helped.

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い at the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. One of the meanings of 安 is cheap , so this is just that as an adjective, cheap . Time to go to a 100 円 shop and get some 安い goods, ammiright?
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: "Would you like this item for cheap ?" " YAASS ( やす ), please!"

sentences.japanese: カメルーンのフルーツはとても安い。
sentences.english: Fruit in Cameroon is very cheap.

sentences.japanese: 私は安いホテルでも平気ですよ。
sentences.english: I'm fine with a cheap hotel.

sentences.japanese: 日本一安いスーパーマーケットへ、ようこそ！
sentences.english: Welcome to the cheapest supermarket in Japan!

meaningMnemonic: The middle country ... who could that be? Let's think about it. Who invented kanji and therefore probably thinks they're the middle of the world? Who also is just a huge country that ruled much of Asia? That would be none other than China .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just make sure you watch out for the rendaku.

sentences.japanese: 中国の人口は日本よりも大きい。
sentences.english: China's population is larger than Japan.

sentences.japanese: 中国には有名な山がたくさんあります。
sentences.english: There are many famous mountains in China.

sentences.japanese: 私のマッサージの先生は中国人です。
sentences.english: My massage instructor is a Chinese person.

meaningMnemonic: The company leader is the company president . Be sure to greet your 社長 with a hearty good morning when they stumble in!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 社長はミーティング中です。
sentences.english: The company president is in a meeting.

sentences.japanese: コウイチはトーフグという会社の社長なんですよ。
sentences.english: Koichi is the president of a company called Tofugu.

sentences.japanese: 社長は、中国やアメリカに手を広げ、小さい会社をグローバルビジネスにしました。
sentences.english: The company president has expanded his company to China and the United States, and turned a small company a global business.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: Tell me about your country . Now imagine that everyone in your country has coo l knee s ( くに ). That's because the national dress code is shorts, so everyone's knees get chilly. That why they have cool knees. You could also imagine cool knees in the sense of trendy knees. What makes for cool knees, in your opinion?

sentences.english: current state of the nation, how the nation ought to be

sentences.japanese: 私はブルガリアという国の生まれです。
sentences.english: I was born in a country called Bulgaria.

sentences.japanese: この国は夜に女の人が一人で出かけても安全ですよ。
sentences.english: This country is safe for a woman to go out alone at night.

meaningMnemonic: Writing has change d our entire culture . In fact, when someone reads a good piece of writing it changes them, and changes their culture too. What writing has changed you so much it has changed your culture and the way you act?
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 文 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: In your culture , everyone drives bun car s ( ぶんか ). Indeed, bun cars are the height of culture. And because they're made out of buns, they're much less dangerous.

sentences.english: a culture center, a civic center

sentences.japanese: これは日本の文化についての本です。
sentences.english: This is a book about Japanese culture.

sentences.japanese: この町の古い文化を外国人にも知ってほしいんです。
sentences.english: I want foreigners to know the old culture of this town.

sentences.japanese: コスプレは日本の文化の一つですか？
sentences.english: Is cosplaying part of Japanese culture?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji for death and body put together make for a dead body . Hopefully you don't have to use or see this vocab too much.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: a corpse rises, a corpse surfaces (in a body of water, etc.)
to see a dead body, to view the body

sentences.english: The dead bodies of the two were found in the mountains.

sentences.japanese: 牛の死体が、土の中にあります。
sentences.english: A cow corpse is in the ground.

sentences.japanese: あの車のトランクに死体が入ってます。
sentences.english: There is a corpse in the trunk of that car over there.

sentences.japanese: その死体のオデコにはワニカニのステッカーがはられていた。
sentences.english: There was a WaniKani sticker stuck to that corpse's forehead.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

sentences.japanese: その死は早すぎました。
どうして死がこわくないの？
sentences.english: Why are you not afraid of death?

sentences.japanese: ペットの死は本当につらいものだ。
sentences.english: It is really tough to lose a pet.

meaningMnemonic: The way you say things is your dialect . It's an entire "way" of speaking. You can even think of the 方 as being a "direction." If you go far enough in different directions in a country, you'll discover different regional dialects.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: このエリアの方言で「ありがとう」は何と言いますか？
sentences.english: How do you say "thanks" in the dialect of this area?

sentences.japanese: この国では方言がとても大切にされています。
sentences.english: In this country, dialects are cherished.

sentences.japanese: 日本の方言を学ぶことは、日本文化を大切にすることです。
sentences.english: Learning Japanese dialects is valuing Japanese culture.

meaningMnemonic: The direction yonder over there is still just the direction of something, though a complicated way to say it, I think. This direction is the "what direction did he go in?" sort of direction.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.english: life direction, the course of one's life

sentences.japanese: 入り口の方向はどちらですか。
あの山の方向に月が見えます。
sentences.english: You will be able to see the moon in the direction of that mountain over there.

sentences.japanese: 男は、コンビニの方向に走った。
sentences.english: The man ran to the direction of the convenience store.

meaningMnemonic: ドル is the Japanese version of the English word dollar . The dollar symbol $ is also common in Japanese, and the pronunciation is still ドル .

sentences.japanese: それって米ドル？それともカナダドル？
sentences.english: Is that U.S. dollars? Or is it Canadian dollars?

sentences.japanese: ついにドル円のレートが１ドル＝１５０円になった。
sentences.english: The dollar to yen rate finally reached 150 yen to the dollar.

meaningMnemonic: This is the adverb version of the kanji early . It's a little thing you can begin sentences with to say you're doing something early or quickly .
readingMnemonic: Since you already know the reading of the vocab word 早い , you should be able to read this word as well.

sentences.english: a little faster, a little sooner

sentences.japanese: 平日は早く会社に行きます。
sentences.english: I go to work early on weekdays.

sentences.japanese: 三日も早くメールが来た。
sentences.english: I got an email three days earlier.

sentences.japanese: ゆっくり休んで早くよくなってください。
sentences.english: Please get plenty of rest and feel better soon.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with the kanji, but here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: You see a man walk straight toward the sun rising in the east . It's so bright he can't see anything, so he trips and he gash es ( ひがし ) his knee on a rock. Yikes… But he gets back up, determined to head east, and, oh no, he gashes his other knee! OK, he should probably give up on going east.

sentences.english: to be located to the east

sentences.japanese: ノースカロライナはアメリカの東にあります。
sentences.english: North Carolina is located in east of the United States.

sentences.japanese: ここから東へ行くと、川がありますよ。
sentences.english: If you go east from here, there is a river.

sentences.japanese: それでは、東の方を向いて下さい。
sentences.english: Then, please turn to the east.

meaningMnemonic: Remember 北口 and 西口 from a few levels before? This is the east version of that, so it means east exit or east entrance .
readingMnemonic: Just like 北口 and 西口 , this also uses kun'yomi readings. And just like before, watch out for the rendaku that changes くち to ぐち !

sentences.english: to be at the east exit
to be at the east exit
to exit to the east gate

sentences.japanese: 東口にはコンビニがありますか？
sentences.english: Is there a convenience store at the east exit?

sentences.japanese: バスは東口から出ます。
sentences.english: Buses leave from the east exit.
Let's meet at the east exit.

meaningMnemonic: If you have lively energy you have more than enough energy for everyone to start noticing. They come up to you and compliment you on your amazing liveliness .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just be careful because かつ is being shortened here to かっ . It's a pretty common change for on'yomi ending in つ , so keep your eyes open for more that do this!

sentences.english: to be enveloped in vigor, to be bustling

sentences.japanese: この町は、とても活気があります。
マイケルのおかげで、会社に活気が生まれた。
sentences.english: Thanks to Michael, liveliness was brought to the company.

sentences.japanese: ファーマーズマーケットはいつも活気にあふれています。
sentences.english: The farmers market is always full of life.

meaningMnemonic: You have ten part s out of ten. Which means you have quite enough . The amount you have is sufficient and plenty .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to understand sufficiently, to know enough

sentences.japanese: 十分なコミュニケーション
あなたは十分がんばりました！
ここには十分なスペースがありません。
sentences.english: There is not enough space here.

sentences.japanese: 十分に考えたんですか？
sentences.english: Have you thought this through enough?

meaningMnemonic: Your origin partner is a partner you had originally, but don't have anymore. In other words, this is your ex-partner or former partner . Like in English, this word is fairly formal, and it covers any kind of ex-partner, including business and romantic partners.
readingMnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi of 元 and then it's just kana, so you should know how to read this!

sentences.japanese: あなたの元パートナー
フランス人の元パートナー

sentences.english: a former partner of the prince

sentences.japanese: 元パートナーからテキストがきた。
sentences.english: I got a text from my ex-partner.

sentences.japanese: あ、それ、元パートナーのネックレスといっしょだ。
sentences.english: Oh, it's the same as my ex-partner's necklace.

sentences.japanese: これは、ふじ山で元パートナーとスキーをしたときのビデオだよ。
sentences.english: This is a video of me skiing with my ex-partner at Mt. Fuji.

meaningMnemonic: When you have a name (that is known to people) or you have famous ness, you are probably someone who is famous .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: ニコラス・ケイジは日本でも有名です。
sentences.english: Nicholas Cage is famous in Japan too.

sentences.japanese: 日本で有名な山と言えば、ふじ山です。
sentences.english: What's known as a famous mountain in Japan is Mt. Fuji.

sentences.japanese: 有名人に会ったことある？
sentences.english: Have you ever met a celebrity?

meaningMnemonic: When you have a fast mouth , you're probably a fast talker , right motormouth?
readingMnemonic: Remember how body parts often change even jukugo words to kun'yomi readings? That's what happened here too. Both readings are kun'yomi, making this one はやくち .

sentences.english: to rapidly pour out a litany of speech
hard to understand because of fast speech
to rapidly pour out a litany of speech
My brother is very fast talker.

sentences.japanese: 早口でオーダーしたので、生ビールが一つの代わりに五つ来た。
sentences.english: I spoke fast when I made an order, so I got five beers instead of one.

sentences.japanese: 日本人は、早口が上手な人が多いですね。
sentences.english: Many Japanese are good at fast-talking.

meaningMnemonic: An outside country is one outside of your own country. That is a foreign country , other countries , or overseas .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to be in a foreign country
to be in a foreign country
to go to a foreign country

sentences.japanese: まだ外国に行ったことがありません。
sentences.english: I have never been to a foreign country yet.

sentences.japanese: 日本生まれの母にとって、「ハグ」は外国の文化です。
sentences.english: For my Japanese-born mother, “hugging” is a foreign culture.

sentences.japanese: ホノルルは、あまり外国っていう気がしません。
sentences.english: Honolulu doesn't feel like a foreign country.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. It's basically a polite way to say something died ( 死ぬ ).

meaningMnemonic: Remember 広い ? Well this is like that, except a verb. When something does the action of getting wide , it means to spread out , to extend , or to stretch . You already learned 広げる , which is used when you spread SOMETHING. But 広がる is intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. Like: The sea spreads out before you. See? No direct object. Actually, verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある , it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 広い , too, so as long as you knew that you knew this reading as well.
